## Monday asked who is recognized

Monday's answer was that presence is not influence, and that a process without
shared influence tends to produce decisions that do not hold.

<br>

Today asks the mechanical follow-up: **what determines whether influence can be
shared at all?**

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §5.2. Governance is the machinery that turns
Chapter 4's commitments into law, policy, funding, authority, and everyday
practice.

**Pacing.** Full deck is 54 minutes; the core path is 48. Slides marked "If time
is short, skip this slide" are the drop list: Box 5.1 and the funding slide.
Protect the last three: the pair rehearsal is the direct rehearsal for Friday
item 2, and the Friday slide carries the case-brief reading expectation.
:::

## Today's question

Who can act, who must be involved, and what constraints shape the decision?

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 5, §5.2. The chapter states this as the
practical question for students and professionals. Write it on the board; it is
the spine of the whole class and of Friday's item 2.
:::

## What you should be able to do

By the end of today, you should be able to:

- define governance and distinguish it from an agency's day-to-day action;
- name the four foundations and apply the good-governance criteria;
- identify the authority, implementation, accountability, and relationship
  questions in a real decision; and
- explain how funding operates as a governance mechanism.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 5, §§5.2--5.6. These map onto the four sections
of class and onto Friday's four response items.
:::

## Governance is not background {.section-slide background-color="#2f6b57"}

It determines what management is allowed, expected, and able to do.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 5, §5.2. This is the chapter's own framing:
governance is at the core of management, not peripheral to it.
:::

## What governance means

Governance is the interplay of **rules, policies, institutions, and powers**
that guide decision-making, implementation, and enforcement.

<br>

A biologist may identify a habitat problem, harvest concern, disease risk, or
access need. The response depends on statutes, budgets, commissions, courts,
Tribal authority, landownership, public support, and administrative capacity.

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §5.2. Ask students to name a management
action and then list what would have to be true for it to happen. The list they
produce is a governance analysis.
:::

The figure illustrates how legal authority flows from beneficiaries to trust administrators." height=490}

Trace three things: **decision-making · implementation · enforcement**

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §5.2 and Figure 5.1. Use the alt text as the

## Four foundations, four questions

  | Foundation              | The question it answers                                    |
  | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Deliberative democracy  | Who gets a voice?                                          |
  | Public trust thinking   | Who owns or benefits from wildlife?                        |
  | Sustainable use         | How much use is sustainable?                               |
  | Precautionary principle | How should agencies act when the risk of inaction is high? |

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §§5.3.1--5.3.1.4. Take each in turn. For
deliberative democracy, note that direct democracy also shapes wildlife policy:
Arkansas's 1997 conservation sales tax, California's 1998 trapping prohibition,
Colorado's 2020 wolf reintroduction. For precaution, use the Atlantic cod
collapse and the 21 species delisted as extinct in 2023.
:::

## The foundations can pull against each other

<br> <br>

::: {.key-idea}
A decision can seek participation, public benefit, sustainable use, and caution
under uncertainty at the same time --- and those aims can point in different
directions.
:::

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §5.3.2. The chapter is explicit: democracy
may require more than public comment when publics lack time, trust, language
access, or confidence that input matters. Precaution can justify restraint but
also requires monitoring, thresholds, and willingness to act before all
uncertainty is removed.
:::

## Seven tenets of the North American Model

1. Wildlife is conserved and held in **public trust** for all citizens.
2. Commerce in dead wildlife is eliminated.
3. Wildlife is allocated by the democratic **rule of law**.
4. Wildlife may be killed only for a legitimate, non-frivolous purpose.
5. Wildlife is an **international resource**.
6. Everyone has equal opportunity under the law to hunt and fish.
7. **Scientific management** guides wildlife conservation.

::: notes
Source: Chapter 5, Box 5.1. These are the seven principles of the North American
Model of Wildlife Conservation, summarized from the assigned reading.
:::

## Critiques the North American Model

A **historical summary** of how wildlife management developed, largely from the
1920s through the 1950s. Seven principles, with wildlife as a public trust at
the core.

Critiques it has drawn:

- continued biodiversity loss and nongame decline;
- a strong emphasis on hunting, fishing, and game;
- limited recognition of Tribal and First Nations rights and perspectives; and
- limited attention to nonconsumptive users, animal welfare, and spiritual
  significance.

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, Box 5.1. The key distinction: the model is
descriptive, the ten contemporary principles are normative. The critiques do not
make it irrelevant; they show why governance must ask who benefits, who
participates, and which species and values receive attention.

**If time is short, skip this slide.** The thread survives without it.
:::

## Good governance is more than biological success

Chapter 5 offers ten criteria that can be clustered into six qualities

1. responsive
2. inclusive of diverse perspectives
3. transparent and accessible
4. accountable 5. sustainable and
5. adaptable
6. coordinated across boundaries

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §§5.3.2--5.3.3. Ask which quality would be
hardest to assess and why. Then ask the chapter's own warning: what happens when
principles remain performative? Publics hear broad commitments but cannot see
how those commitments shaped the decision, and frustration increases.
:::

## Governance in action {.section-slide background-color="#123f5a"}

Decisions are distributed across overlapping jurisdictions, not located in a
single office.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 5, §5.4. This is why authority, coordination,
access, and conflict are central to the profession.
:::

## Who holds authority

- **Federal:** migratory birds, threatened and endangered species, marine
  mammals, interstate commerce; NEPA applies to federal lands, federal funding,
  or ESA-listed species.
- **Tribes and First Nations:** sovereign entities with inherent rights, their
  own programs, commissions, and law enforcement.
- **States, provinces, territories:** broad authority within their borders under
  the state ownership doctrine; commissions of 4--19 members typically set
  regulations.
- **Courts:** the 2024 ruling overturning the Chevron Doctrine shifted
  interpretation of ambiguous statutes from agency experts to judges.

::: notes
Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §§5.4.1--5.4.3 and §§5.5.1--5.5.3. Spend the
most time on the Tribal row: at least 56.2 million acres held in trust; the
Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 and the Indian Self-Determination and
Education Assistance Act of 1975; missions that often prioritize cultural and
subsistence use. Note the chapter's own caution that treaty rights and
consultation requirements need legal sources and cannot be inferred from an
acreage summary.
:::

## Most habitat is not public

About **60%** of land in the United States is privately owned. In Nebraska, it
is roughly **97%**.

- Landowners do not own the wildlife on their property; the public trust
  doctrine still applies.
- Conservation is rarely a legal obligation without an instrument such as a
  conservation easement.
- So governance reaches private land mostly through **incentives**: CRP and WRP
  (1985), Forest Legacy (1990), EQIP and CSP (1996), Working Lands for Wildlife
  (2012).

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §5.5.4. For a Nebraska class this is the
single most consequential slide of the day. If 97% of the state is private, then
voluntary, incentive-based governance is not a supplement to management here ---
it is the main instrument.
:::

## Funding is a governance mechanism

Funding shapes what agencies can do, who they answer to, and which work is
feasible.

- Federal excise-tax programs support state fish and wildlife work.
- State, Tribal, Canadian, NGO, and mitigation sources create other pathways.
- Diverse revenue expands capacity --- and each source carries its own
  constraints and expectations.

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §5.6. Connect back to Monday's Box 4.3: the
2023 Columbia Basin settlement mattered because it moved control of restoration
funds toward Tribal governments. Who holds the money is a governance question.

**If time is short, skip this slide.** The thread survives without it.
:::

## Collaboration and comanagement

::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%"}
**Collaboration**

People work together to find common ground, solve problems, and respond to
conflict. May or may not hold decision authority.
:::::
::::: {.column width="50%"}
**Comanagement**

A formal or informal arrangement in which **sovereign entities** share
responsibility and authority.
:::::
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, Box 5.2. The distinction matters for Friday:
two of the three options in the case brief are collaboration, one is
comanagement. Comanagement is available only where a sovereign partner exists.
:::

## What makes collaboration hold

- Engage every relevant interest; work to understand others' interests.
- Make sure participants know their **BATNA** --- best alternative to a
  negotiated agreement.
- Send representatives who are knowledgeable **and empowered** by their
  organizations.
- Share control where appropriate.
- Build trust by following through on commitments.
- Treat partnerships as long-term relationships.

::: {.key-idea}
Its weakness: one participant can undermine the process if they believe they
have more to gain by doing so. Participants must have something to lose and
something to gain.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, Box 5.2. Define BATNA plainly: what each
party gets if they walk away. Ask students which party in Friday's case brief
has the strongest BATNA --- that party is the hardest to keep at the table.
:::

## Four practical questions for any decision

1. **Authority:** Who can make or change the decision?
2. **Implementation:** Who has to carry it out?
3. **Accountability:** Who can evaluate or challenge the decision?
4. **Relationships:** Which governments, publics, and partners must be involved
   for the decision to work?

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §§5.2--5.3. Use as a checklist, not a claim
that every decision has the same answers. Friday's response item 2 asks for
exactly this map.
:::

## Pair rehearsal: make one governance claim

With a partner, complete this claim about Friday's case:

> The decision is made by \_\_\_\_\_\_ under the constraint of \_\_\_\_\_\_. It
> cannot be implemented without \_\_\_\_\_\_. One party that can challenge or
> block it is \_\_\_\_\_\_.

::: notes
Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 5, §§5.4--5.5. Two minutes to draft, then hear
two claims. Push on the last blank: the ability to challenge a decision is the
accountability mechanism, and students routinely leave it blank. This is direct
rehearsal for Friday item 2.
:::
